# Toon et al. 1989 two-stream, as implemented {#sec-ch04}

This chapter documents pyharp's two-stream solver, selected by `solver: toon` in a band's YAML, which follows
Toon et al. [-@reading02]. The same solver object runs one of two kernels: without the `planck` flag it is a shortwave solver
for a collimated beam (quadrature closure with delta-Eddington scaling, @sec-ch04-shortwave); with `planck` it is a
longwave solver for thermal emission (hemispheric-mean closure with the source-function technique,
@sec-ch04-longwave), which needs the band-integrated Planck function of @sec-ch04-planck. Both build one
tridiagonal system per column. The option `zenith_correction` is accepted but has no effect (@sec-ch04-zenith).
Notation follows @sec-ch02; the accuracy of the closures against the full radiative transfer equation is the
subject of @sec-ch05. Where the solver sits in a flux calculation, between the solver input of a band and the sum
over its spectral points, is described in @sec-ch01-pipeline.

### Summary

The shortwave solver turns the optical properties of a column of layers, a collimated beam from above and a
reflecting surface into upward and downward fluxes at every layer interface. It solves the two-stream equations
of Toon et al. [-@reading02] exactly for layers whose optical properties are constant, so the only
approximation is the two-stream closure itself; this section shows which closure the code uses and where
round-off enters.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Diffuse and direct shortwave fluxes of a layered column; @eq-ch04-shortwave-ode with the gammas of
@eq-ch04-shortwave-gammas.

**Data.** Per layer $\Delta\tau_n$, $\omega$, $g$ (dimensionless); beam $F_0$ [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$], $\mu_0$, $A_s$; out:
$F^+$ and $F^- + F_{\mathrm{dir}}$ [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$] at levels and layer midpoints.

**Placement.** Called by the band solver for every wavenumber and column; one tridiagonal solve per column.

**Activation.** `solver: toon` in a band, without the `planck` flag. Always quadrature closure, always
delta-Eddington.

**Guarantee / limits.** Exact solution of the two-stream system to round-off for $\lambda\Delta\tau_n \lesssim 15$;
see the Limits layer of @sec-ch04-shortwave.

**Evidence.** The Tests layer of @sec-ch04-shortwave.
:::

Local symbols (not in the notation of @sec-ch02): $\xi$, the optical depth below the top of a layer;
$E_{1n},\dots,E_{4n}$, the unscaled interface coefficients
of the code; $x_{\mathrm{cap}} = 35$, the cap on $\lambda\Delta\tau_n$; $e_F$, the flux error measure of the tests.

The scheme has no switches of its own. It always applies delta-Eddington scaling with truncation fraction $f = g^2$
and always uses the quadrature closure ($\mu_1 = 1/\sqrt{3}$). The interface values are exact for the two-stream
system; the error against the full radiative transfer equation is the closure error that @sec-ch05 measures. The
code calls the solver `toon_mckay89`; YAML selects it with `solver: toon`.

### Derivation

The radiative transfer problem and its notation are those of @sec-ch02, and the two-stream closure family is that
of @sec-ch02-closures. Optical
depth $\tau$ is measured downward from the top of the atmosphere; layers are numbered $n = 1,\dots,L$ from the top;
inside layer $n$ a local depth $\xi \in [0, \Delta\tau_n]$ is measured from the layer top.

**Scaling.** The code first replaces $\omega$, $g$ and $\Delta\tau_n$ by their delta-Eddington values (the
transform of @eq-ch02-delta-scaling-transform, in the notation of @sec-ch02-delta-scaling)
[@reading06] with truncation fraction $f = g^2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\omega^{\mathrm{s}} &= \frac{(1 - f)\,\omega}{1 - \omega f}, \\
\Delta\tau^{\mathrm{s}}_n &= (1 - \omega f)\,\Delta\tau_n, \\
g^{\mathrm{s}} &= \frac{g - f}{1 - f} = \frac{g}{1 + g}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-shortwave-delta}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch04-shortwave-delta shortwave_check.py [C3] -->

@eq-ch04-shortwave-delta is computed in `toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).
The last equality follows from $f = g^2$: $(g - g^2)/(1 - g^2) = g(1 - g)/((1 - g)(1 + g))$. The scaling keeps the
absorption optical depth, $(1 - \omega^{\mathrm{s}})\Delta\tau^{\mathrm{s}}_n = (1 - \omega)\Delta\tau_n$, and removes the forward peak
$f\omega\Delta\tau_n$ from the scattering optical depth. From here on every quantity is the scaled one and the
superscript $\mathrm{s}$ is dropped.

**Equations.** With the direct beam $F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau) = \mu_0 F_0 e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$ as the source, the diffuse
fluxes in layer $n$ obey [@reading02, eqs. 11-14]

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}F^+}{\mathrm{d}\tau} &= \gamma_1 F^+ - \gamma_2 F^- - \gamma_3\,\omega F_0\,e^{-\tau/\mu_0}, \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}F^-}{\mathrm{d}\tau} &= \gamma_2 F^+ - \gamma_1 F^- + \gamma_4\,\omega F_0\,e^{-\tau/\mu_0},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-shortwave-ode}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch04-shortwave-ode shortwave_check.py [C2] -->

with the quadrature coefficients of Toon et al. [-@reading02, Table 1]

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_1 &= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\bigl(2 - \omega(1 + g)\bigr), \\
\gamma_2 &= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,\omega(1 - g), \\
\gamma_3 &= \frac{1 - \sqrt{3}\,g\,\mu_0}{2}, \\
\gamma_4 &= 1 - \gamma_3.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-shortwave-gammas}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch04-shortwave-gammas shortwave_check.py [C1] -->

@eq-ch04-shortwave-gammas is computed as `g1`, `g2`, `g3`, `g4` in `toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).

**Homogeneous solution.** Without the beam term, try $(F^+, F^-) = (u, v)\,e^{s\tau}$ in @eq-ch04-shortwave-ode:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\gamma_1 - s)\,u - \gamma_2\,v &= 0, \\
\gamma_2\,u - (\gamma_1 + s)\,v &= 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

A nonzero $(u, v)$ needs a zero determinant, $-(\gamma_1 - s)(\gamma_1 + s) + \gamma_2^2 = 0$, so $s = \pm\lambda$
with

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= \sqrt{\gamma_1^2 - \gamma_2^2}, \\
\Gamma &= \frac{\gamma_1 - \lambda}{\gamma_2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-shortwave-eigen}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch04-shortwave-eigen shortwave_check.py [C1] -->

For $s = -\lambda$ the first row gives $u/v = \gamma_2/(\gamma_1 + \lambda)$, and multiplying numerator and
denominator by $\gamma_1 - \lambda$ gives $u/v = (\gamma_1 - \lambda)/\gamma_2 = \Gamma$; for $s = +\lambda$ the
second row gives $v/u = \Gamma$ in the same way. @eq-ch04-shortwave-eigen is computed as `lam` and `gam` in
`toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}); the
check `[C1]` of `shortwave_check.py` verifies both relations symbolically.

**Particular solution.** Try $(F^+, F^-) = (C^+, C^-)$ with $C^\pm = c^\pm e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$. Substituting into
@eq-ch04-shortwave-ode and dividing by $e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{c^+}{\mu_0} &= \gamma_1 c^+ - \gamma_2 c^- - \gamma_3\,\omega F_0, \\
-\frac{c^-}{\mu_0} &= \gamma_2 c^+ - \gamma_1 c^- + \gamma_4\,\omega F_0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first row gives $c^- = \bigl((\gamma_1 + 1/\mu_0)\,c^+ - \gamma_3\omega F_0\bigr)/\gamma_2$. Putting this into
the second row and collecting $c^+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_2 c^- &= (\gamma_1 + 1/\mu_0)\,c^+ - \gamma_3\,\omega F_0, \\
(\gamma_1 - 1/\mu_0)\,\gamma_2 c^- &= \gamma_2^2 c^+ + \gamma_4\gamma_2\,\omega F_0, \\
(\gamma_1^2 - 1/\mu_0^2)\,c^+ - \gamma_3(\gamma_1 - 1/\mu_0)\,\omega F_0 &= \gamma_2^2 c^+ + \gamma_4\gamma_2\,\omega F_0,
\end{aligned}
$$

where the second line is the second row multiplied by $\gamma_2$, and the
third line replaces $\gamma_2 c^-$ on its left by the first line, multiplied by $\gamma_1 - 1/\mu_0$.
With $\lambda^2 = \gamma_1^2 - \gamma_2^2$, and by the same steps for $c^-$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C^+(\tau) &= \omega F_0\,\frac{(\gamma_1 - 1/\mu_0)\,\gamma_3 + \gamma_2\gamma_4}{\lambda^2 - 1/\mu_0^2}\,e^{-\tau/\mu_0}, \\
C^-(\tau) &= \omega F_0\,\frac{(\gamma_1 + 1/\mu_0)\,\gamma_4 + \gamma_2\gamma_3}{\lambda^2 - 1/\mu_0^2}\,e^{-\tau/\mu_0}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-shortwave-particular}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch04-shortwave-particular shortwave_check.py [C2] -->
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch04-shortwave-particular shortwave_check.py [C7] -->

@eq-ch04-shortwave-particular is Toon et al. [-@reading02, eqs. 23-24] with $\pi F_s = F_0$; it is computed as
`Ap`, `Am`, `Cpm1`, `Cmm1`, `Cp`, `Cm` in `toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).
Check `[C2]` of `shortwave_check.py` substitutes both lines back into @eq-ch04-shortwave-ode and gets zero, and
check `[C7]` confirms that the second line of the elimination above is the second row multiplied by $\gamma_2$. The
denominator vanishes at $\lambda\mu_0 = 1$; the code's treatment is in the Numerical method layer of @sec-ch04-shortwave.

**Layer solution.** In layer $n$, with the local depth $\xi$ and $\tau = \tau_{n-1} + \xi$ ($\tau_{n-1}$ the depth of
the layer top), the general solution is the homogeneous part plus @eq-ch04-shortwave-particular:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_n^+(\xi) &= k_{1n}\,e^{\lambda_n \xi} + \Gamma_n k_{2n}\,e^{-\lambda_n \xi} + C_n^+(\tau_{n-1} + \xi), \\
F_n^-(\xi) &= \Gamma_n k_{1n}\,e^{\lambda_n \xi} + k_{2n}\,e^{-\lambda_n \xi} + C_n^-(\tau_{n-1} + \xi).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-shortwave-layer}

@eq-ch04-shortwave-layer is Toon et al. [-@reading02, eqs. 19-20] written from the layer top; it is evaluated
at $\xi = 0$ and $\xi = \Delta\tau_n$ as `FLX_UP` and `FLX_DN` in `toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).
Together with the conditions below it is checked end to end by `toon_pyharp_check.py` `[C1]`-`[C3]`.
The code's unknowns are $Y_{2n-1} = (k_{1n} + k_{2n})/2$ and $Y_{2n} = (k_{1n} - k_{2n})/2$, so that
$k_{1n} = Y_{2n-1} + Y_{2n}$ and $k_{2n} = Y_{2n-1} - Y_{2n}$ (`xk1`, `xk2`). Unlike Toon et al. [-@reading02,
eqs. 29-32], the code does not rescale them by $e^{\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n}$; the consequence is in
the Limits layer of @sec-ch04-shortwave.

**Boundary and interface conditions.** No diffuse light enters at the top, the fluxes are continuous at every
interior interface, and the surface reflects the diffuse and direct downward flux with albedo $A_s$
[@reading02, eqs. 33-37]:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_1^-(0) &= 0, \\
F_n^\pm(\Delta\tau_n) &= F_{n+1}^\pm(0), \quad n = 1,\dots,L-1, \\
F_L^+(\Delta\tau_L) &= A_s\,\bigl(F_L^-(\Delta\tau_L) + F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau_L)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-shortwave-bc}

@eq-ch04-shortwave-bc is assembled as the rows `Af`, `Bf`, `Cf`, `Df` in `toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).

**What is exact and what is truncated.** For layers of constant $\omega$, $g$, the interface fluxes solve the
two-stream system exactly; the delta-Eddington scaling and the quadrature closure are the approximation, and their
error against the full equation belongs to @sec-ch05. The boundary and interface conditions are checked end to end by
`toon_pyharp_check.py` `[C1]`-`[C3]` (pyharp against a 40-digit solution of @eq-ch04-shortwave-ode); the symbolic
identities of the equations above are in `shortwave_check.py`, as tagged next to each equation.

### Numerical method

Writing @eq-ch04-shortwave-bc with @eq-ch04-shortwave-layer gives $2L$ linear equations in the $2L$ unknowns
$Y_l$. The top condition is the first row, the surface condition the last, and each interior interface gives two
rows: the code forms the sum and the difference of the two continuity conditions so that each row couples only the
neighbouring unknowns. The result is tridiagonal (@fig-ch04-shortwave-system), with coefficients built from

$$
E_{1n} = e^{\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n} + \Gamma_n e^{-\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n},\quad
E_{2n} = e^{\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n} - \Gamma_n e^{-\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n},
$$

$$
E_{3n} = \Gamma_n e^{\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n} + e^{-\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n},\quad
E_{4n} = \Gamma_n e^{\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n} - e^{-\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n},
$$

where each exponent is capped, $\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n \leftarrow \min(\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n, x_{\mathrm{cap}})$
with $x_{\mathrm{cap}} = 35$. The system is solved by the Thomas algorithm in `dtridgl` ({{< code src/rtsolver/dtridgl_impl.h dtridgl repo=pyharp >}}):
one forward elimination, one back substitution, no pivoting; a pivot that is exactly zero is replaced by
$10^{-12}$.

**Where quantities live.** $\Delta\tau_n$, $\omega$, $g$ are layer values; fluxes are level values. pyharp stores
layers and levels bottom to top (array index 0 at the surface), and the kernel reverses the order on read
(`DTAU_IN`, `FLX_UP` in `toon_mckay89_shortwave`, {{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}}).
The direct beam uses the scaled optical depth, $F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau) = \mu_0 F_0 e^{-\tau^{\mathrm{s}}/\mu_0}$, and is added
to the downward channel, which therefore holds $F^- + F_{\mathrm{dir}}$.

**Resonance.** The denominator of @eq-ch04-shortwave-particular vanishes at $\lambda_n\mu_0 = 1$. The fluxes are
smooth in $\mu_0$ there, but $c^\pm$ grow like $1/(\lambda_n\mu_0 - 1)$ and cancel in the solve. When
$|\lambda_n\mu_0 - 1| < \sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}}$ the code moves that layer's $\mu_0$ to
$(1 \pm \sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}})/\lambda_n$, a relative change of $\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}}$
($1.5\times10^{-8}$ in double precision, check `[C6]` of `shortwave_check.py`). Toon et al. [-@reading02,
p. 16290] recommend the same remedy.

**Midpoints.** The midpoint channels hold the layer solution @eq-ch04-shortwave-layer at $\xi = \Delta\tau_n/2$ for
the diffuse part, and the geometric mean $\sqrt{F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau_{n-1})F_{\mathrm{dir}}(\tau_n)}$ for the
beam, which is exact for an exponential.

**Pure absorption.** When every layer has $\omega \le 10^{-12}$ and $A_s \le 10^{-12}$, the code skips the solve
and returns the unscaled Beer-Lambert beam $\mu_0 F_0 e^{-\tau/\mu_0}$ in the downward channel and zero upward.
In a column that does scatter, a layer with $\gamma_2 = 0$ exactly ($\omega = 0$) gets $\gamma_2 = 10^{-10}$ instead
(`g2` in `toon_mckay89_shortwave`), so that $\Gamma = (\gamma_1 - \lambda)/\gamma_2$ stays finite.

The cost is one pass over the layers to form the coefficients, one tridiagonal solve of $2L$ rows and one pass to
evaluate the fluxes: $O(L)$ per column and wavenumber. Columns and wavenumbers are independent; the CPU dispatch
runs them in parallel through `call_toon89_sw_cpu` ({{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_sw_cpu repo=pyharp >}}).

: Code map of the shortwave solver. {#tbl-ch04-shortwave-code}

1. `ToonMcKay89Impl::forward` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89.cpp ToonMcKay89Impl::forward repo=pyharp >}}) requires
   `prop` of rank 4 (wavenumber, column, layer, property) and pads a property axis shorter than 3 with zeros
   ($\omega = g = 0$). It reads `umu0` (shape: columns; default 1), `fbeam` (wavenumber x column; default 0) and
   `albedo` (wavenumber x column; default 0), each optionally prefixed by the band name, and refuses other shapes
   with a `TORCH_CHECK` error.
2. `umu0` is broadcast to every level of a column; the kernel's per-level slant path is therefore never taken
   (@sec-ch04-zenith).
3. `call_toon89_sw_cpu` ({{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_sw_cpu repo=pyharp >}}) runs
   `toon_mckay89_shortwave` per column and wavenumber in float or double; it ignores `top_emission_flag`,
   `btop_factor`, `hard_surface` and `delta_eddington_lw`.
4. `toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}})
   applies @eq-ch04-shortwave-delta, forms @eq-ch04-shortwave-gammas, @eq-ch04-shortwave-eigen and
   @eq-ch04-shortwave-particular, assembles @eq-ch04-shortwave-bc, calls `dtridgl`, and writes the four output
   channels.

A band selects this solver in YAML with `solver: toon` and no `planck` in its `flags`; the band also gives its
`name`, its `range` and `nwave` in the list `bands`. These keys are parsed in `RadiationBandOptionsImpl::from_yaml`
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandOptionsImpl::from_yaml repo=pyharp >}}).

: Tests of the shortwave solver. {#tbl-ch04-shortwave-tests}

The tests of `tests/test_toon.cpp` (ctest `test_toon.release`) run on CPU and, in a CUDA build, on the GPU; the
runs quoted here are CPU only. With $e_F = \max|F^{\mathrm{pyharp}} - F^{\mathrm{ref}}|/(F_0\mu_0)$ over every
level and both channels, the check gives $e_F = 4.0\times10^{-10}$ for single layers (worst case $\Delta\tau = 10$,
$\omega = 0.3$, $\mu_0 = 0.6$) and $e_F$ below $10^{-12}$ for 7 and 50 sublayers, 216 cases each[^ch04-sw-grid]. At
the resonance $e_F = 1.9\times10^{-8}$, the size of the guard's shift[^ch04-sw-grid]. The five cases of Toon et al.
[-@reading02, Table 4] reproduce the printed two-stream fluxes within $3.5\times10^{-4}$, inside the rounding of
three printed decimals[^ch04-sw-grid]. The symbolic identities `[C1]`-`[C7]` of `shortwave_check.py` all

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
A single layer with $\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n \gtrsim 20$ at the bottom of the column loses accuracy at the surface;
$\omega = 1$ passed directly to `ToonMcKay89` gives wrong fluxes.
:::

- **Unscaled exponentials (CANDIDATE, thick bottom layer).** Because the amplitudes are not rescaled by
  $e^{\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n}$, the solve carries $e^{\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n}\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}$ round-off
  (@fig-ch04-shortwave-thick-layer): $e_F$ is $4.5\times10^{-8}$ at $\lambda\Delta\tau = 20$,
  $9.9\times10^{-4}$ at 30, and $0.15$ from the cap at 35 upward[^ch04-sw-thick]. In a column the error appears only
  at the surface level below a thick bottom layer: with layers $(0.5, 0.5, 30)$ from the top, $\omega = 0.3$,
  $\mu_0 = 0.6$, the surface fluxes are $F^+ = -2.2\times10^{-2}$ and $F^- + F_{\mathrm{dir}} = -2.0\times10^{-3}$
  (per unit $F_0$) instead of values below $10^{-19}$ with the bottom layer split into 400 sublayers; the top
  fluxes agree to $10^{-16}$, and a thick layer with thinner layers below it shows no error[^ch04-sw-thick].
  Splitting thick bottom layers avoids it.
- **$\omega = 1$ (CANDIDATE, conservative scattering).** At $\omega^{\mathrm{s}} = 1$, $\gamma_1 = \gamma_2$, so $\lambda = 0$,
  $\Gamma = 1$ and the interface coefficient $1 - \Gamma^2$ vanishes (check `[C4]` of `shortwave_check.py`); the
  system is singular and `dtridgl` replaces the zero pivot by $10^{-12}$. With $\omega = 1$ exactly,
  Toon Table 4 case 1 returns $F^+(0) = 3.1411 \approx \mu_0 F_0$ (all incident light reflected) instead of $0.174$, and
  $e_F = 1.1$; with $\omega = 1 - 10^{-12}$, $e_F = 1.6\times10^{-11}$[^ch04-sw-thick]. The band solver caps
  $\omega$ at $1 - \delta\omega$ before calling the kernel (@sec-ch07), so the defect is reachable only by calling
  `ToonMcKay89` directly.
- **Untested combinations.** Variable $\mu_0$ per level is unreachable (@sec-ch04-zenith). Float32 runs are covered
  only by the tests of @tbl-ch04-shortwave-tests at their single-precision tolerances; the checks of this section

### Summary

The longwave solver computes the thermal-emission fluxes of a layered column from the temperatures at its levels.
It runs in two stages, following the source-function technique of Toon et al. [-@reading02]. A hemispheric-mean
two-stream solve fixes the scattering source in every layer. Then the radiative transfer equation is integrated
exactly along five directions, down from the top and up from the surface. The second stage makes the result exact
for a non-scattering layer whose Planck function is linear in optical depth, up to the five-point angular rule.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Thermal $F^\pm$ of a layered column; the source function of @eq-ch04-longwave-source integrated by
@eq-ch04-longwave-sweep.

**Data.** Per layer $\Delta\tau_n$, $\omega$, $g$; level temperatures $T$ [K]; band edges $\nu$
[$\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$]; $A_s$. Out: $F^\pm$ [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$] at levels and layer midpoints.

**Placement.** Called by the band solver for every wavenumber and column; one tridiagonal solve, then ten sweeps.

**Activation.** `solver: toon` with `planck` in `flags`; options `hard_surface`, `delta_eddington_lw`,
`top_emission_flag` (default 0), `btop_factor` (default $e^{-1}$).

**Guarantee / limits.** Isothermal column in equilibrium to round-off with `hard_surface` and
`top_emission_flag: 1`; see
the Limits layer of @sec-ch04-longwave.

**Evidence.** The Tests layer of @sec-ch04-longwave.
:::

Local symbols (not in the notation of @sec-ch02): $\xi$, the optical depth below the top of a layer;
$\eta_1$, $\eta_2$, two square roots used once in the Derivation; $a = \sqrt{(1-\omega)/(1-\omega g)}$ (the notation rules of @sec-ch02
name it $a$; code `alp`); $\tau^\star = 1/(\gamma_1+\gamma_2)$; $G, H, J, K, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \sigma_1,
\sigma_2$ of Toon et al. [-@reading02, Table 3] in the code's normalisation; $s_{\mathrm{top}}$ and
$b_{\mathrm{top}}$ for the options `top_emission_flag` and `btop_factor`; $\rho_n$ for the optional `area_scale`.

The defaults are: no delta scaling, no diffuse light entering at the top ($s_{\mathrm{top}} = 0$), and a surface
that emits the Planck function of the bottom level extrapolated with the layer gradient (`hard_surface` off).
Every option is listed in @tbl-ch04-longwave-code. The internal name is `toon_mckay89_longwave`.

### Derivation

Notation and the radiative transfer equation are those of @sec-ch02; $\tau$ increases downward, layers
$n = 1,\dots,L$ are counted from the top, and $\xi \in [0, \Delta\tau_n]$ is the depth inside layer $n$.

**Planck function.** The code takes $B$ linear in optical depth inside each layer:

$$
\begin{aligned}
B_n(\xi) &= B_{0n} + B_{1n}\,\xi, \\
B_{0n} &= \bar B(T_{n-1/2}), \\
B_{1n} &= \bigl(\bar B(T_{n+1/2}) - \bar B(T_{n-1/2})\bigr)/\Delta\tau_n,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-longwave-planck}

with $T_{n-1/2}$ and $T_{n+1/2}$ the temperatures at the top and bottom of layer $n$ and $\bar B$ the band radiance
of @sec-ch04-planck. For $\Delta\tau_n \le 10^{-6}$ the code sets $B_{1n} = 0$ and $B_{0n}$ to the mean of the two
level values. @eq-ch04-longwave-planck is computed as `B0` and `B1` in `toon_mckay89_longwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}}).
This is Toon et al. [-@reading02, eqs. 25-26].

**Closure.** The hemispheric mean assumes an isotropic intensity in each hemisphere and a phase function equal to
$1 + g$ forward and $1 - g$ backward [@reading02, Table 1], so $\mu_1 = 1/2$ and (as in
@eq-ch02-closures-hm-a)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma_1 &= 2 - \omega(1 + g), \\
\gamma_2 &= \omega(1 - g), \\
\lambda &= \sqrt{\gamma_1^2 - \gamma_2^2} = \frac{a\,(1 - \omega g)}{\mu_1}, \\
\Gamma &= \frac{\gamma_2}{\gamma_1 + \lambda} = \frac{1 - a}{1 + a}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-longwave-closure}

The two right-hand forms are the ones the code uses (`lam`, `gam` in `toon_mckay89_longwave`,
{{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}}). This $\Gamma$ is the same
quantity as $(\gamma_1 - \lambda)/\gamma_2$ of @eq-ch04-shortwave-eigen; the two forms are equal. They follow from
$\gamma_1 = (1-\omega) + (1-\omega g)$ and $\gamma_2 = (1-\omega g) - (1-\omega)$: then
$\gamma_1^2 - \gamma_2^2 = 4(1-\omega)(1-\omega g) = 4a^2(1-\omega g)^2$, and with $\eta_1 = \sqrt{1-\omega g}$,
$\eta_2 = \sqrt{1-\omega}$,
$\Gamma = (\eta_1^2 - \eta_2^2)/(\eta_1 + \eta_2)^2 = (\eta_1 - \eta_2)/(\eta_1 + \eta_2) = (1 - a)/(1 + a)$. Check `[C1]` of `longwave_check.py`
verifies both on 90 exact points.

**Particular solution.** In the infrared the two-stream equations of @eq-ch04-shortwave-ode carry the source
$S = 2\pi(1 - \omega)B_n(\xi)$ in place of the beam terms [@reading02, eq. 15]:
$\mathrm{d}F^+/\mathrm{d}\xi = \gamma_1 F^+ - \gamma_2 F^- - S$ and $\mathrm{d}F^-/\mathrm{d}\xi = \gamma_2 F^+ - \gamma_1 F^- + S$.
Try $F^\pm = c^\pm + d\,\xi$. The terms in $\xi$ and the constant terms of the two equations give

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 &= (\gamma_1 - \gamma_2)\,d - 2\pi(1-\omega)B_{1n}, \\
d &= \gamma_1 c^+ - \gamma_2 c^- - 2\pi(1-\omega)B_{0n}, \\
d &= \gamma_2 c^+ - \gamma_1 c^- + 2\pi(1-\omega)B_{0n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the hemispheric mean $\gamma_1 - \gamma_2 = 2(1-\omega)$, so the first line gives $d = \pi B_{1n}$.
Subtracting the third line from the second gives $c^+ + c^- = 2\pi B_{0n}$, and adding them gives
$c^+ - c^- = 2d/(\gamma_1 + \gamma_2)$ (check `[C8]` of `longwave_check.py`). Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_n^\pm(\xi) &= \pi\,\bigl(B_{0n} + B_{1n}(\xi \pm \tau^\star)\bigr), \\
\tau^\star &= \frac{1}{\gamma_1 + \gamma_2} = \frac{\mu_1}{1 - \omega g}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-longwave-particular}

@eq-ch04-longwave-particular is Toon et al. [-@reading02, eq. 27] ($2\pi\mu_1 = \pi$); the code stores it divided
by $\pi$ as `Cpm1`, `Cmm1`, `Cp`, `Cm` and $\tau^\star$ as `term` in `toon_mckay89_longwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}}),
and solves for the homogeneous amplitudes $k_{1n}$, $k_{2n}$ in the same units. The layer solution, the interface
conditions and the tridiagonal system are those of @eq-ch04-shortwave-layer and @eq-ch04-shortwave-bc with
@eq-ch04-longwave-particular in place of the beam term, and with these end rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_1^-(0) &= \pi B_{\mathrm{top}}, \\
F_L^+(\Delta\tau_L) &= A_s F_L^-(\Delta\tau_L) + \pi S_s,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-longwave-bc}

where $B_{\mathrm{top}} = s_{\mathrm{top}}\bar B(T_{1/2})$ for $s_{\mathrm{top}} \ge 0$ (only 0 and 1 are meaningful;
larger values scale the top source) and
$B_{\mathrm{top}} = (1 - e^{-b_{\mathrm{top}}\Delta\tau_1/\mu_1})\,\bar B(T_{1/2})$ for $s_{\mathrm{top}} < 0$; and
$S_s = (1 - A_s)\,\bar B(T_{L+1/2})$ with `hard_surface`, $S_s = \bar B(T_{L+1/2}) + B_{1L}\mu_1$ without it.
@eq-ch04-longwave-bc is assembled as the first and last rows of `Af`, `Bf`, `Cf`, `Df` in `toon_mckay89_longwave`
({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}}).

::: {#prp-ch04-longwave-isothermal}
For an isothermal column ($B_{1n} = 0$, $B_{0n} = B$), $s_{\mathrm{top}} = 1$ and `hard_surface`, every right-hand
side of the tridiagonal system vanishes, so $k_{1n} = k_{2n} = 0$ and $F^\pm = \pi B$ at every level, for any
$\omega$, $g$ and $A_s$.
:::

The top row has right-hand side $B - B = 0$, each interface row has $C_{n+1}^\pm(0) - C_n^\pm(\Delta\tau_n) = 0$, and
the bottom row has $(1 - A_s)B - B + A_s B = 0$; check `[C4]` of `longwave_check.py` does this symbolically. Without
`hard_surface` the bottom right-hand side is $B - B + A_s B = A_s B$ (check `[C5]`), so the proposition needs
$A_s = 0$ there.

**Source function.** With the two-stream fluxes known, the hemispheric-mean source function of the
azimuth-integrated intensity is, for upward ($+$) and downward ($-$) directions,

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\pi S_n^+(\xi) &= \omega\,\bigl[(1+g)F_n^+ + (1-g)F_n^-\bigr] + 2\pi(1-\omega)B_n(\xi), \\
2\pi S_n^-(\xi) &= \omega\,\bigl[(1+g)F_n^- + (1-g)F_n^+\bigr] + 2\pi(1-\omega)B_n(\xi).
\end{aligned}
$$

Inserting the layer solution in the code's normalisation, $F_n^+ = \pi\,(k_{1n}e^{\lambda\xi} + \Gamma k_{2n}e^{-\lambda\xi}) + C_n^+$
and $F_n^- = \pi\,(\Gamma k_{1n}e^{\lambda\xi} + k_{2n}e^{-\lambda\xi}) + C_n^-$ ($k_{1n}$, $k_{2n}$ in units of $F/\pi$), and
collecting the factors of $e^{\lambda \xi}$ uses
$(1 + g) + (1 - g)\Gamma = 2(1 + g a)/(1 + a)$ and $(1 + g)\Gamma + (1 - g) = 2(1 - g a)/(1 + a)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\pi S_n^+(\xi) &= G\,e^{\lambda \xi} + H\,e^{-\lambda \xi} + \alpha_1 + \alpha_2 \xi, \\
2\pi S_n^-(\xi) &= J\,e^{\lambda \xi} + K\,e^{-\lambda \xi} + \sigma_1 + \sigma_2 \xi, \\
G &= 2\pi\omega k_{1n}\,\frac{1 + g a}{1 + a}, \\
H &= 2\pi\omega k_{2n}\,\frac{1 - g a}{1 + a}, \\
J &= 2\pi\omega k_{1n}\,\frac{1 - g a}{1 + a}, \\
K &= 2\pi\omega k_{2n}\,\frac{1 + g a}{1 + a}, \\
\alpha_1 &= 2\pi\bigl(B_{0n} + \omega g\,\tau^\star B_{1n}\bigr), \\
\sigma_1 &= 2\pi\bigl(B_{0n} - \omega g\,\tau^\star B_{1n}\bigr), \\
\alpha_2 &= \sigma_2 = 2\pi B_{1n}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-longwave-source}

@eq-ch04-longwave-source is Toon et al. [-@reading02, eqs. 53-54 and Table 3] in the code's normalisation, computed
as `g`, `h`, `xj`, `xk`, `alpha1`, `alpha2`, `sigma1`, `sigma2` in `toon_mckay89_longwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}});
for $\omega \le 10^{-4}$ the code drops the scattering terms ($G = H = J = K = 0$, $\alpha_1 = \sigma_1 = 2\pi B_{0n}$).
Check `[C6]` of `longwave_check.py` verifies the coefficients symbolically.

**Angular sweeps.** Along a direction $\mu > 0$ the azimuth-integrated intensities obey
$\mu\,\mathrm{d}I^+/\mathrm{d}\tau = I^+ - 2\pi S^+$ and $-\mu\,\mathrm{d}I^-/\mathrm{d}\tau = I^- - 2\pi S^-$.
Integrating across layer $n$ with an integrating factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_n^+(0) &= I_n^+(\Delta\tau_n)\,e^{-\Delta\tau_n/\mu} + \int_0^{\Delta\tau_n} 2\pi S_n^+(\xi)\,e^{-\xi/\mu}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\xi}{\mu}, \\
I_n^-(\Delta\tau_n) &= I_n^-(0)\,e^{-\Delta\tau_n/\mu} + \int_0^{\Delta\tau_n} 2\pi S_n^-(\xi)\,e^{-(\Delta\tau_n - \xi)/\mu}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\xi}{\mu}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch04-longwave-sweep}

The integrals of the four terms of @eq-ch04-longwave-source are elementary; for example the $G$ term of the upward
sweep is $G\,(e^{(\lambda - 1/\mu)\Delta\tau_n} - 1)/(\lambda\mu - 1)$. All six closed forms are those of Toon et al.
[-@reading02, eqs. 55-56], and are evaluated in `toon_mckay89_longwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}});
check `[C7]` of `longwave_check.py` integrates them with sympy and compares them with these plain-quotient forms (the
forms the code uses for $\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n \ge 35$; the `exprel` forms used below 35 are not covered by a check). The top value is
$I_1^-(0) = 2\pi B_{\mathrm{top}}$, with $\mu_1$ replaced by $\mu$ for $s_{\mathrm{top}} < 0$; the surface value is
$I_L^+ = 2\pi(1 - A_s)\bar B(T_{L+1/2}) + 2A_s F^-(\tau_L)$ with `hard_surface` (a Lambertian reflector) and
$2\pi(\bar B(T_{L+1/2}) + B_{1L}\mu)$ without it. The fluxes are

$$
F^\pm = \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i\,I^\pm(\mu_i),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i = \tfrac12,
$$ {#eq-ch04-longwave-flux}

with $\mu_i$, $w_i$ the five-point Gauss rule for the weight $\mu$ on $[0, 1]$, so that
$F = \int_0^1 I\,\mu\,\mathrm{d}\mu$ is exact for $I$ polynomial of degree 9 in $\mu$. @eq-ch04-longwave-flux is
computed with `uarr`, `wuarr` in `toon_mckay89_longwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_longwave repo=pyharp >}});
check `[C3]` recomputes the rule and matches the ten stored digits.

**What is exact and what is truncated.** The sweeps are exact for the source of @eq-ch04-longwave-source; for
$\omega = 0$ that source is the exact one, so the only errors are the linear-in-$\tau$ Planck function and the
five-point angular rule. With scattering, the source carries the hemispheric-mean closure error (@sec-ch05).

### Numerical method

The tridiagonal system has the shape of @fig-ch04-shortwave-system and is solved by `dtridgl`
({{< code src/rtsolver/dtridgl_impl.h dtridgl repo=pyharp >}}). Its coefficients use the same unscaled exponentials capped at
$\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n = 35$ as the shortwave solver. The sweeps run as @fig-ch04-longwave-sweep shows: for each
of the five angles, one downward pass from the top boundary value and, after the surface value is formed from the
downward flux, one upward pass. The level fluxes accumulate $w_i I^\pm(\mu_i)$; the midpoint channels accumulate the
same expressions evaluated at $\xi = \Delta\tau_n/2$.

::: {#cell-fig-ch04-longwave-sweep .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4}

Step 2 (orange, solid): the intensity is integrated down from the top along five directions. Step 3 (green, dashed): it is integrated up from the surface along the same directions. The fluxes are the weighted sums at the right.](04-toon_files/figure-html/fig-ch04-longwave-sweep-output-1.svg){#fig-ch04-longwave-sweep fig-alt='A stack of four layers labelled with B0n plus B1n tau; five solid orange arrows pointing down and five dashed green arrows pointing up beside it; a formula for the flux as the weighted sum of intensities with weights summing to one half.'}

**Near-resonant directions.** The closed forms of @eq-ch04-longwave-sweep contain $1/(\lambda\mu - 1)$. For
$\lambda_n\Delta\tau_n < 35$ the code evaluates them as $x\,\mathrm{exprel}(\delta x)$ with
$\mathrm{exprel}(y) = (e^y - 1)/y$ (`longwave_exprel`, {{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_longwave_impl.h longwave_exprel repo=pyharp >}}),
which is finite and accurate at $\lambda\mu = 1$; above it uses the plain quotient, which is singular at
$\lambda\mu = 1$ and inaccurate near it (defect P12, Limits layer).

**Where quantities live.** As in the Numerical method layer of @sec-ch04-shortwave, arrays run bottom to top and the kernel reverses them.
$\bar B$ is evaluated at the levels from the level temperatures `temf`; the surface value is that of the bottom
level. When the boundary data carry `area_scale` $\rho$ (one value per level, $(r/r_{\mathrm{ref}})^2$), the level
Planck values are multiplied by it before the kernel runs, so the result is the $\rho$-weighted flux and the caller
divides by the same factor.

The cost is $O(L)$ for the solve plus $O(5L)$ for the sweeps per column and wavenumber, run in parallel over both by
`call_toon89_lw_cpu` ({{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_lw_cpu repo=pyharp >}}).

### Summary

The longwave solver needs the Planck function of every level integrated over a band of wavenumbers. pyharp
computes that integral from two short series in the dimensionless variable $v = c_2\nu/T$, instead of by
quadrature. This section derives both series, states what the routine returns (a radiance, per steradian), and
measures its accuracy.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** $\bar B = \int_{\nu_1}^{\nu_2} B_\nu\,\mathrm{d}\nu$ from @eq-ch04-planck-band.

**Data.** Band edges $\nu_1 \le \nu_2$ [$\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$]; $T > 0$ [K]; out $\bar B$
[$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,sr^{-1}}$].

**Placement.** Once per call of the longwave solver, for every level and wavenumber.

**Activation.** Always with the `planck` flag; the band edges are the band's `range`.

**Guarantee / limits.** Within $6\times10^{-5}$ relative of the integral for four bands at 300 K; equal edges are
wrong by $10^{10}$ (Limits layer of @sec-ch04-planck).

**Evidence.** The Tests layer of @sec-ch04-planck.
:::

Local symbols (not in the notation of @sec-ch02): $v = c_2\nu/T$; $c_1$, $c_2$ the radiation constants as the
code writes them; $\Phi(v)$ the fraction of $\sigma T^4/\pi$ emitted below $v$; $\Phi_c(v) = 1 - \Phi(v)$.

The routine has no options. Its header documents the result as a flux [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$]; it is the radiance,
$1/\pi$ of the hemispheric flux, and the longwave solver uses it as a radiance, so the solver's fluxes are right
(Limits layer of @sec-ch04-planck). The series are those of DISORT's `PLKAVG`, whose C port in the DISORT 2.1.3 code
bundled with pydisort is `c_planck_func1` ({{< code cdisort213/cdisort.c c_planck_func1 repo=pydisort >}}). pyharp
differs from it in three ways: it always sums six exponential terms where `c_planck_func1` uses up to seven for
$v < 1.9$, it has no Simpson-rule branch for narrow bands, and it leaves an edge with $v = 1.5$ exactly in neither
series (defect P11, Limits layer).

### Derivation

The Planck radiance per wavenumber $\nu$ [$\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$] is $B_\nu = 2hc^2\nu^3/(e^{c_2\nu/T} - 1)$ with
$c_2 = hc/k$. Substituting $x = c_2\nu/T$ and using $\int_0^\infty x^3/(e^x - 1)\,\mathrm{d}x = \pi^4/15$:

$$
\bar B = \int_{\nu_1}^{\nu_2} B_\nu\,\mathrm{d}\nu = \frac{\sigma T^4}{\pi}\,\bigl(\Phi(v_2) - \Phi(v_1)\bigr),\qquad
\Phi(v) = \frac{15}{\pi^4}\int_0^{v}\frac{x^3}{e^x - 1}\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$ {#eq-ch04-planck-band}

@eq-ch04-planck-band is computed in `bbflux_wavenumber` ({{< code src/radiation/bbflux.cpp bbflux_wavenumber overload=2 repo=pyharp >}}).

**Small $v$.** With the Bernoulli expansion $x/(e^x - 1) = 1 - x/2 + x^2/12 - x^4/720 + x^6/30240 - x^8/1209600
+ \dots$, multiplying by $x^2$ and integrating term by term:

$$
\Phi(v) = \frac{15}{\pi^4}\,v^3\Bigl(\frac13 - \frac{v}{8} + \frac{v^2}{60} - \frac{v^4}{5040} + \frac{v^6}{272160}
- \frac{v^8}{13305600}\Bigr) + O(v^{13}).
$$ {#eq-ch04-planck-small}

**Large $v$.** With $1/(e^x - 1) = \sum_{m\ge1} e^{-mx}$ and
$\int_v^\infty x^3 e^{-mx}\,\mathrm{d}x = e^{-mv}\bigl(v^3/m + 3v^2/m^2 + 6v/m^3 + 6/m^4\bigr)$:

$$
\Phi_c(v) = 1 - \Phi(v) = \frac{15}{\pi^4}\sum_{m=1}^{6} \frac{e^{-mv}}{m^4}\bigl((mv)^3 + 3(mv)^2 + 6mv + 6\bigr)
+ O\bigl(e^{-7v}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-ch04-planck-large}

@eq-ch04-planck-small and @eq-ch04-planck-large are the coefficients `A1`-`A6` and the loop over `m` in
`bbflux_wavenumber` ({{< code src/radiation/bbflux.cpp bbflux_wavenumber overload=2 repo=pyharp >}}). The code uses the first
for $v < 1.5$ and the second for $v > 1.5$ (an edge with $v = 1.5$ exactly is in neither, so its $\Phi$ and
$\Phi_c$ are both 0), and forms $\bar B$ from $\Phi(v_2) - \Phi(v_1)$ when both are small,
$1 - \Phi(v_1) - \Phi_c(v_2)$ when they straddle 1.5, and $\Phi_c(v_1) - \Phi_c(v_2)$ when both are large (@fig-ch04-planck-series).

**What is exact and what is truncated.** Both series are truncated. At $v = 1.5$ the first neglected term of
@eq-ch04-planck-small, $(15/\pi^4)(5/66)\,v^{13}/(13\cdot 10!)$, is $5\times10^{-8}$ of $\sigma T^4/\pi$, and the
$m = 7$ term of @eq-ch04-planck-large is $3\times10^{-6}$ (check `[C6]` of `planck_check.py`); the exponential
tail therefore sets the truncation error near the switch. That $m = 7$ term is dropped because pyharp sums a fixed
six terms; the PLKAVG port keeps it for $v < 1.9$. The constants are
also rounded: $c_2 = 1.438786$ cm K against $hc/k = 1.4387769$ cm K, and $\sigma = 5.67032\times10^{-8}$ against
$5.670374419\times10^{-8}$ $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$. The check is `planck_check.py`, a line-for-line numpy port.

A reader who sets `zenith_correction` expects the shortwave solver to account for a beam cosine that changes with
height, as in a spherical atmosphere. pyharp accepts the option and reports it, but no code reads it, and the
shortwave kernel never receives a cosine that varies with height.

The option is parsed: `ToonMcKay89OptionsImpl::zenith_correction` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89.hpp ToonMcKay89OptionsImpl::zenith_correction repo=pyharp >}})
returns true when `zenith_correction` is among the `flags`, and `RadiationBandOptionsImpl::from_yaml`
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandOptionsImpl::from_yaml repo=pyharp >}}) appends it to the flags when a
band's `toon:` block sets `zenith_correction: true`. `ToonMcKay89Impl::forward`
({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89.cpp ToonMcKay89Impl::forward repo=pyharp >}}) passes the value to the dispatch, where
`call_toon89_sw_cpu` ({{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_sw_cpu repo=pyharp >}}) takes the parameter and
does not use it; `call_toon89_lw_cpu` ({{< code src/rtsolver/rtsolver_dispatch.cpp call_toon89_lw_cpu repo=pyharp >}}) leaves it
unnamed.

The kernel `toon_mckay89_shortwave` ({{< code src/rtsolver/toon_mckay89_shortwave_impl.h toon_mckay89_shortwave repo=pyharp >}})
does contain a branch for a cosine that differs between levels: it accumulates the slant optical depth layer by
layer and uses the mean of the two level cosines in the particular solution. That branch is unreachable, because
`ToonMcKay89Impl::forward` accepts `umu0` only with one value per column and expands that value to every level
before the kernel runs. With the flag on and off, the shortwave fluxes of a 30-layer test column are bitwise
equal (CANDIDATE, zenith correction; check `[K1]`)[^ch04-zenith-k1].

The behaviour lives nowhere in the solver at the pin. A caller that needs height-dependent geometry must scale the
fluxes outside the solver; the Radiation API's spherical treatment is described in @sec-ch08.
